title: How the network was trained
lead: The network started as random numbers. It learned in two stages: first it copied the classical engine, then it played against itself and learned from its own games. This page explains both stages, the data-science words behind them, and what the seven loop runs achieved and what they did not.

sec.overview.title: Two stages
sec.overview.p1: The {term:neural-network|network} of {sec:inference/network-basics|topic 3} begins with random weights. Training turns it into a player in two stages. Stage one is {term:supervised-learning}: the classical engine plays, and the network learns to predict its moves and the game results. The result is {term:generation} 0. Stage two is a {term:self-play} loop in the style of AlphaZero: the best network plays itself with {term:mcts|MCTS}, a candidate learns from those games, and a match called the {term:gate} decides whether the candidate replaces the best network.
sec.overview.p2: Seven {term:loop-run|loop runs} were made: training runs of the self-play loop, each with its own settings, numbered 1 to 7. Together they ran for about 38 hours on one Apple M3 Max, until a stop criterion that had been fixed in advance was met. Since then, the network engines in the app get stronger through search, not through more training: their strength setting is the number of MCTS {term:simulation|simulations} per move.
sec.overview.p3: Keep two networks apart. The last network trained is the LARGE network of loop run 4, generation 11; it is not part of the repository. The browser ships {term:small-large|SMALL} networks: the expert model from loop run 3, generation 13, and a shared model for all four variants (two or three players, neighbour jump or long hop) that was trained in stage one only. The default browser engine is still the classical alpha-beta search of {sec:classical/alpha-beta|topic 2}.
sec.samples.title: What a training sample is
sec.samples.p1: A {term:training-sample} is one labelled row of data: an input and the answers the network should give for it. The input is a position: the 121 cells, seen from the side to move, plus the ply and the move limit. The answers are two {term:target|targets}. The {term:policy} target gives every legal move a probability, so it says how good each move looks. The {term:value} target is the expected game result for each player, from −1 (loss) to +1 (win). Two weights per sample can switch a target off; a random opening move, for example, teaches no policy.
sec.samples.p2: On disk a sample is small: a measured 479 bytes, with 52.5 legal moves on average, for classical games at {n:1000} nodes. The samples sit in {term:safetensors} files of 25 to 50 games each, written by {src:selfplay/src/main/java/sternhalma/selfplay/SampleFile.java}. The {term:input-plane|input planes} that the network reads are not stored. `SampleExpander` rebuilds them from the cells when it assembles a batch, much as you would expand a compact DTO into the object a method needs.
sec.teacher.title: Generation 0: learning from the classical engine
sec.teacher.p1: Generation 0 learns from {term:best-spec|BEST_SPEC}, the strongest classical player: the alpha-beta search of topic 2 with its {sec:classical/evaluation|learned evaluation}. `BEST_SPEC` plays the games. A second search computes the exact score of every legal move at a fixed depth, and a {term:softmax} with the teacher temperature `tau` (0.1 at depth 3) turns these scores into the policy target ({src:selfplay/src/main/java/sternhalma/selfplay/Teacher.java}). The value target mixes the game result with the search score. At ply 0 the search score weighs 70 %, at ply 100 only 30 %, because early in a game the final result is a noisy label. The documentation calls this schedule a first choice, not a measured optimum.
sec.teacher.p2: More data helped more than more steps. Run 1 of generation 0 trained on {n:4300} games for 4 {term:epoch|epochs}, and its raw policy (the network's favourite move, no search) lost to the engine at depth 1: −49 ± 64 Elo. The verdict was that data, not steps, was the limit. Run 2 used {n:20000} games from a depth-3 teacher, about 1.9 million samples, and its raw policy beat depth 1 by +38 ± 45 Elo ({src:selfplay/src/main/java/sternhalma/selfplay/Gen0.java}).
sec.teacher.p3: Run 3 repeated run 2 with the same data and the same batches, and changed one thing: classical input planes and two residual priors ({sec:inference/trunk-heads|topic 3}). It reached the same {term:kl-divergence} in about half the steps, and its raw policy scored +135 Elo more than run 2 against depth 1. This variant, `classic1`, became the default.
sec.learning.title: Loss, gradient and learning rate
sec.learning.p1: Training needs one number that says how wrong the network is: the {term:loss}. For the policy the project uses the {term:cross-entropy} between the network's move probabilities and the target. It reports the KL divergence, which is the cross-entropy minus a part that only depends on the target, and is 0 exactly when both distributions agree. For the value it uses the {term:mse|mean squared error}. The loss of a {term:batch} is the average over its samples, 256 per step here. Think of a test that does not pass or fail, but returns a score you want to push down.
sec.learning.p2: For each of the about {n:62000} weights of the SMALL network, the {term:gradient} says in which direction, and how strongly, the loss changes when that weight grows. {term:backpropagation|Backpropagation} computes all gradients in one pass backwards through the layers, with the chain rule. {term:gradient-descent|Gradient descent} then moves every weight a small step against its gradient. The size of that step is the {term:learning-rate}: too large and the loss jumps around, too small and training crawls. The {term:optimiser} that turns gradients into updates is {term:adamw|AdamW}. It scales each weight's step by the size of its recent gradients, and it shrinks the weights slightly at every step ({term:weight-decay}) ({src:nn/src/main/java/sternhalma/nn/Optimizer.java}).
sec.learning.p3: The learning rate changes during a run ({src:nn/src/main/java/sternhalma/nn/LearningRateSchedule.java}). A {term:warm-up} raises it linearly over the first steps; a {term:cosine-decay} then lowers it along half a cosine curve to a small final value. Loop run 2 used a constant {sci:3e-4} (0.0003) and stalled: it rejected three generations in a row. A sweep outside the loop found the cause. On the same data, a cosine from {sci:3e-4} to {sci:1e-5} over {n:15000} steps beat the start network clearly, while {n:15000} constant steps did worse. {sec:tuning/recipe-sweep|Topic 5} tells how the sweep was run.
sec.loop.title: One generation of the self-play loop
sec.loop.p1: One generation has four phases: self-play, training, gate and decision ({src:selfplay/src/main/java/sternhalma/selfplay/Loop.java}). In self-play the best network plays itself with {sec:inference/mcts|MCTS}, in loop runs 2 to 4 with {n:2500} games and 200 simulations per move. To make the games differ, {term:dirichlet-noise} is added to the network's priors at the root, and in the first 14 plies the move is drawn in proportion to the visit counts ({term:temperature} 1). The policy target of a position is the share of simulations each move received; the value target is the game result, never a search value ({src:selfplay/src/main/java/sternhalma/selfplay/LoopGame.java}).
sec.loop.p2: The samples go into a {term:replay-buffer}: a window of the most recent samples in memory that evicts the oldest whole generation, like a bounded queue ({src:selfplay/src/main/java/sternhalma/selfplay/ReplayBuffer.java}). Training draws random batches from the whole window, so the network does not forget older games, and mirrors two-player samples left to right at random ({term:data-augmentation}). The candidate starts from the best network's weights with a fresh AdamW optimiser. The {term:reuse-factor} R sets the number of steps: `steps = ceil(R · new samples / batch)`.
sec.loop.p3: The gate plays the candidate against the best network in pairs of games from the same random opening, with the colours swapped ({src:selfplay/src/main/java/sternhalma/selfplay/Gate.java}). The candidate is promoted only if `score − 1.28 · se > 0.5`, where se is the {term:standard-error} of the pair scores: better than even with 90 % one-sided confidence. The plain rule “score above 0.5” would promote half of all candidates that are only equally strong. A rejected candidate is discarded; its games stay in the window.
sec.throughput.title: Virtual threads and one GPU thread
sec.throughput.p1: MCTS evaluates one leaf at a time, but a GPU wants many positions at once. Collecting several leaves inside one search did not work: on the CPU, a batch of 16 cost 325 Elo at 100 simulations ({term:virtual-loss}), and the CPU {term:forward-pass} gains nothing from batches. So the batch comes from many games instead. 256 games in flight hand their next position to one `PooledEvaluator` ({src:nn/src/main/java/sternhalma/nn/PooledEvaluator.java}). Two cohorts alternate: one fills a batch while the GPU computes the other.
sec.throughput.p2: Each game is a virtual thread ({src:selfplay/src/main/java/sternhalma/selfplay/LoopGamesJob.java}). A game that waits for its evaluation parks and costs nothing. With platform threads and a permit, every evaluation cost two context switches, and the measured throughput dropped to a third. The `TornadoNetwork` is not thread-safe, so exactly one thread calls it, like a single writer thread behind a queue. On an idle machine at 200 simulations, the SMALL network played 3.3 games per second on the GPU and 1.35 on the CPU.
sec.throughput.p3: Training moved to the GPU as well, through {term:tornadovm|TornadoVM} ({src:nn-tornado/src/main/java/sternhalma/tornado/TornadoTrainer.java}). The CPU trainer processed about 900 samples per second on 8 threads; the GPU trainer {n:49300} at batch 256, 55 to 68 times as many. A whole generation of loop run 1 gained less: it retrained in 41.8 seconds instead of 22.9 minutes, about 33 times faster.
sec.where.title: Where it ran
sec.where.p1: All training ran on one Apple M3 Max, with JDK 25 and the Metal GPU through TornadoVM. The run directories under `data/` hold samples, {term:checkpoint|checkpoints}, gate games and decisions. They are git-ignored and exist only on that machine. Only packed models reach `web/models/` ({sec:architecture/training|topic 1}).
sec.where.p2: AWS was used only for compatibility tests, not for training ({src:scripts/cloud/aws-spot.sh}). One test checked a CPU with AVX-512, at a cost of about 0.01 USD; two tests checked CUDA on an Nvidia Tesla T4, at about 0.06 and 0.07 USD. On the T4, feeding the network at batch 256 reached about 1.0 to 1.6 times the speed of the M3 Max in the same benchmark.
sec.results.title: What the runs achieved
sec.results.p1: Six things helped. The classical teacher gave a better start than random play. The classical input planes and priors halved the steps to a given KL divergence. The GPU trainer made a generation inside the loop about 33 times faster. The gate got stricter, and the learning-rate decay ended the stall of loop run 2. Offline, more {term:capacity} helped as well: the LARGE network (about {n:353000} weights) beat the best network of loop run 3 by +138 Elo at equal simulations. Inside the loop the gain was smaller, as loop run 4 below shows.
sec.results.p2: Loop run 1 ({term:small-large|SMALL}, 10 generations, CPU trainer, 8 h 45 min) promoted 9 of 10 generations. Against `BEST_SPEC` at {n:25600} nodes it climbed from −19 ± 34 to +267 ± 51 {term:elo|Elo}, with smaller gains in each generation. Loop run 3 (14 generations, 10 h 34 min) rose from +211 ± 35 to +354 ± 54 Elo against {n:102400} nodes at generation 9. Then it reached a {term:plateau}: for SMALL, the recipe was exhausted after 8 to 9 generations. The browser ships generation 13, the last promoted network, at +298 ± 46; the ladder does not separate it from generation 9, because their intervals overlap.
sec.results.p3: Loop run 4 put LARGE into the loop and promoted 5 of 11 generations. Against the classical {term:ladder}, generation 11 showed no measurable gain over generation 0 (+407 against +409 Elo at {n:102400} nodes): at scores of 0.82 to 0.91 the ladder is in {term:saturation} and cannot resolve the difference. The direct match shows +78 ± 19 Elo, not the +140 that the five gates add up to. Loop runs 5 to 7 (LARGE, 800 simulations) promoted nothing; their gates together averaged about +2 Elo. That met the stop criterion ({sec:tuning/pre-registered|topic 5}).
sec.energy.title: What the training cost in energy
sec.energy.p1: For the {term:small-large|SMALL} and LARGE networks of the 5-row board, energy was measured as well as time. Everything ran on one MacBook Pro with an Apple M3 Max; AWS played no part ({sec:training/where|where it ran}). {src:scripts/energy/README.md} read the counters of the laptop's battery controller, which estimate the energy at the wall socket. They cover the whole machine, display included, and refresh about once a minute. Idle, the machine drew 12.7 W; while training, 36 to 49 W. The counters cannot split CPU from GPU, so for that comparison the trainer ran alone for 5.5 to 11 minutes on each, and the result was extrapolated to whole runs.
sec.energy.p2: The rows form two groups. The first holds four measured, complete GPU trainings: teacher data, generation 0 and the {term:self-play} loop, without strength checks; SMALL generation 9 ships in the browser. The second holds only the {term:training-step|training steps}, on the GPU and on a 14-thread CPU. Only LARGE on the GPU is measured; the other three are estimates (≈, about ±22 to 23 %). Per step, the CPU took 36 (SMALL) and 51 (LARGE) times as long as the GPU at similar power. No CPU run checked these estimates, and they omit self-play and gates. LARGE generation 10 cost 4.0 times the energy of SMALL generation 9 (0.177 kWh).
sec.energy.p3: Strength is an {term:elo|Elo} rating on one scale for two players on 5 rows. Level 3 (“Standard”), the classical engine at {n:20000} nodes per move, is 1000; the number is unrelated to chess Elo. A random-effects fit over 53 matches places 25 engine settings on it. Its 95 % {term:confidence-interval|interval} includes the disagreement between matches, not only chance. All bars share the uncertain path to level 3, so overlapping bars do not decide which is stronger. The head-to-head match decides: LARGE generation 10 beats SMALL generation 9 by +131 ± 24 Elo at 200 {term:simulation|simulations} each, but loses by −173 ± 36 Elo at equal CPU time per move.
sec.energy.p4: The ratings hold for this game type only. In the game for three players, rated from tables of one against two, the shared 4-row network stands 334 to 539 Elo higher against the same classical engine than with two players. The two scales therefore stay separate, and no mixed number exists. For people there is no rating, because no human games were recorded. The card “Your strength” in the app names the level whose move quality a player matches; on 4 rows, level 2 corresponds to 838 ± 86 Elo. That is an engine equivalent, not a measured rating. An export of the measured moves is planned.
sec.jobs.title: Restartable jobs
sec.jobs.p1: Each phase is a batch job that you can kill at any time ({src:selfplay/src/main/java/sternhalma/selfplay/Job.java}). It derives its state from the files it has written, such as samples, checkpoints and `decision.json`, not from a progress file. It writes files atomically. It holds a lock through `FileChannel.tryLock`; when another run holds the lock, the process ends with the exit code “already running” (75). On SIGINT or SIGTERM it stops between items, prints its SUCCESS, SKIP, ERROR and CLEANUP counts, and ends with the exit code “aborted by SIGINT” (130) or “aborted by SIGTERM” (143).
sec.jobs.p2: A killed run that restarts produces the same bits as a run that was never interrupted. Each batch is drawn with a random generator seeded from run seed, generation and step, and a checkpoint stores weights and optimiser state every 50 steps or 60 seconds ({src:nn/src/main/java/sternhalma/nn/Checkpoint.java}). You know the pattern from an idempotent message consumer: start it again, and it continues where it stopped ({src:scripts/loop.sh}).
sec.jobs.p3: The next topic, {sec:tuning/what|how the hyperparameters were determined}, shows how settings such as the learning rate, the gate rule and the number of simulations were decided.

fig.loop.title: The self-play loop in loop run 3
fig.loop.desc: A cycle of six stages: self-play, samples, replay window, training, gate and decision. A promoted candidate plays the next self-play. Beside it, a timeline of the 14 generations of loop run 3 shows each gate score against the line at {n:0.5}: filled dots for promoted, hollow dots for rejected generations.
fig.loop.caption: Loop run 3, which ran for 10 h 34 min: 200 game pairs per gate, 8 of 14 generations (about 57 %) promoted. The ladder shows the best network against the classical engine at {n:102400} nodes.
fig.loop.cycle.label: Stages of one generation
fig.loop.stage.selfplay.label: Self-play
fig.loop.stage.selfplay.detail: The best network plays itself with MCTS: {n:2500} games per generation at 200 simulations per move in loop run 3. Dirichlet noise at the root and moves drawn by visit count in the first 14 plies make the games differ.
fig.loop.stage.samples.label: Samples
fig.loop.stage.samples.detail: Each searched position becomes a training sample: the share of visits per move is the policy target, the game result is the value target. A search value is never a target.
fig.loop.stage.window.label: Replay window
fig.loop.stage.window.detail: The window keeps the samples of the latest generations in memory. When it is full, the oldest whole generation leaves. Training draws random batches from the whole window.
fig.loop.stage.training.label: Training
fig.loop.stage.training.detail: The candidate starts from the best network with a fresh AdamW optimiser. In loop run 3 the learning rate fell along a cosine from {sci:3e-4} to {sci:1e-5} within each generation, with reuse factor 20.
fig.loop.stage.gate.label: Gate
fig.loop.stage.gate.detail: The candidate plays the best network in pairs of games from the same random opening, with sides swapped; 200 pairs in loop run 3. It is promoted only if `score − 1.28 · se > 0.5`.
fig.loop.stage.decision.label: Decision
fig.loop.stage.decision.detail: Promoted: the candidate becomes the best network and plays the next self-play. Rejected: the candidate is discarded, the old best network plays on, and the new games stay in the window.
fig.loop.oldrule.toggle: Mark the old rule: score above {n:0.5}
fig.loop.oldrule.note: The old rule would also have promoted generations {gens}. Their scores lie above {n:0.5}, but not by more than 1.28 standard errors, so they may be no stronger than the best network.
fig.loop.timeline.title: Gate score per generation
fig.loop.timeline.desc: Dot plot of the 14 gate scores of loop run 3, from {n:0.483} to {n:0.605}, with a reference line at {n:0.5}. Filled dots are promoted generations, hollow dots rejected ones. The cursor marks the chosen generation.
fig.loop.ladder.title: Strength of the best network
fig.loop.ladder.desc: Dot-and-whisker chart of four points: the best network after generations 0, 5, 9 and 13 against the classical engine at {n:102400} nodes. It rises from +211 to +354 at generation 9 and ends at +298 for generation 13, the shipped network; the intervals of generations 9 and 13 overlap.
fig.pooled.title: Many games, one device thread
fig.pooled.desc: Schematic: game tokens in two cohorts, A and B, hand their next positions to one pooled evaluator. While the device thread computes the batch of one cohort on the GPU, the other cohort fills the next batch. In CPU mode, each game evaluates its own positions.
fig.pooled.caption: Schematic: the drawn number of games is not the real one. Measured on an idle Apple M3 Max at 200 simulations: the SMALL network played {n:3.3} games per second with the GPU and {n:1.35} with 8 CPU threads.
fig.pooled.stepper: One cycle of the two cohorts
fig.pooled.mode.label: Evaluator
fig.pooled.idle: Step forward to follow one cycle in which the two cohorts take turns on the GPU.
fig.pooled.step.1: The games of cohort A each reach a leaf, hand its position to the evaluator and park. A parked virtual thread uses no CPU.
fig.pooled.step.2: The evaluator closes the batch of cohort A and passes it to the device thread, the only thread that calls `TornadoNetwork`.
fig.pooled.step.3: The GPU computes batch A. Meanwhile the games of cohort B search and hand in their positions.
fig.pooled.step.4: The results of batch A come back. The games of cohort A wake up and continue their searches.
fig.pooled.step.5: Batch B goes to the device thread, and cohort A starts to fill the next batch.
fig.pooled.step.6: The GPU computes batch B while cohort A fills. The cohorts alternate, so the GPU has work most of the time.
fig.pooled.cpu.note: On the CPU, each game thread runs its own forward pass, one position at a time, because the CPU gains nothing from batches.
fig.pooled.note.measured: Measured: with platform threads and permits instead of virtual threads, self-play reached only a third of this throughput.
fig.lr.title: Learning-rate schedule
fig.lr.desc: A line plot of the learning rate over the training steps of one run: a linear rise during the warm-up, then a cosine fall to the final rate, or a flat line when the rate stays constant. Sliders set the base rate, the final rate, the warm-up and the number of steps.
fig.lr.caption: Computed with the formula of `LearningRateSchedule.java`. Presets: generation 0 ({sci:1e-3}, warm-up 200, cosine to a tenth); the constant {sci:3e-4} that stalled loop run 2; the sweep 1 winner ({sci:3e-4} cosine to {sci:1e-5}, {n:15000} steps).
fig.energy.title: What the training cost
fig.energy.caption: One MacBook Pro with Apple M3 Max. Energy of the whole machine at the wall socket, display included, so each value is an upper bound for the training. The complete runs leave out the acceptance checks. The CPU rows are estimates and cover the training steps only. Strength is Elo for two players on 5 rows, with level 3 (classical engine, {n:20000} nodes) = 1000, from a random-effects fit over 53 matches. Each bar is a 95 % interval and includes the disagreement between matches. Overlapping bars do not decide which network is stronger; for LARGE against SMALL, the head-to-head match decides.
fig.energy.view.label: Axes
fig.energy.basis.label: Compare strength at
fig.energy.status.energy.sims: Strength against energy at equal simulations: in their head-to-head match LARGE generation 10 beats SMALL generation 9 by +131 Elo, for 4.0 times the energy, so it extends the front.
fig.energy.status.energy.time: Strength against energy at equal time per move: in their head-to-head match LARGE generation 10 loses to the cheaper SMALL generation 9 by −173 Elo and drops off the front, as does LARGE generation 0.
fig.energy.status.time.sims: Strength against time at equal simulations: the points barely move from the energy view, because the machine drew almost the same power in every run.
fig.energy.status.time.time: Strength against time at equal time per move: as on the energy axis, SMALL generation 9 is cheaper and stronger than LARGE generation 10.
fig.energy.status.both: Energy against time: all rows lie close to one line of constant power, and the CPU rows lie far to the right of and above their GPU rows.
fig.energy.desc.energy: Scatter plot of strength in Elo, with level 3 = 1000, against training energy in kWh on a log axis. Points show SMALL and LARGE at generation 0 and at their best generation, each with a vertical bar for its 95 % interval. A triangle shows the head-to-head match against SMALL generation 9, and a step line marks the front. The two CPU rows are dashed vertical lines, because their networks have no rating. All values are in the table below.
fig.energy.desc.time: Scatter plot of strength in Elo, with level 3 = 1000, against training time in hours on a log axis, with the same points, interval bars, triangle, front and CPU lines as the energy view. fig.energy.desc.both: Scatter plot of energy against training time, both on log axes, for all eight rows, inside a band of constant power. Dashed paths join the GPU and the CPU row of each network and carry the factors of time and energy. All values are in the table below.
